summary: Defines text/enriched, a MIME type for email text with simple formatting such as bold and italic, marked up with tags. It was meant to be easy for programs to read and still readable as plain text. It is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: Plain email has no bold or italics. This is a simple way to mark words so a mail program can show them fancy, while other programs still show readable text.

questions: how to format email text in mime
subtitle: A deliberately tiny set of angle-bracket tags for bold, italic and layout in email.

tldr.problem: Plain-text email cannot show bold, italics or indentation, and HTML and SGML were judged too heavy and not widely handled by mail programs.
tldr.mechanism: text/enriched is a MIME text subtype where formatting commands sit in angle brackets, such as bold and italic, with a few simple rules for line breaks and nesting.
tldr.outcome: It obsoletes RFC 1523 and RFC 1563 and was meant only for the short term until other MIME types for text formatting in mail were deployed.

today: RFC 1896 is an Informational RFC that obsoletes RFC 1523 and RFC 1563. It says it is meant for the short term until other MIME types for text formatting in Internet mail are developed and deployed.

sections.title: Goals of text/enriched
sections.content:
text/enriched is a subtype of the MIME content-type "text" for simple formatted text. Its one optional parameter is charset, with the same values as text/plain. The RFC is a minor revision of the type first described in RFC 1523 and RFC 1563.

The design criteria are: the syntax must be extremely simple to parse; it must be extensible; the raw form should be readable enough on a non-MIME reader (for ASCII and 8-bit supersets); and the capabilities must be extremely limited, so what is sent is likely to display properly.

The authors chose it over HTML and SGML because most MIME-aware mail programs could already format it or strip the commands, and because HTML 2.0 had many unneeded features while missing some that text/enriched had. Appendix B of the RFC has a small C program that converts to HTML 2.0.
sections.plainLanguage: The authors wanted formatting so simple that even very basic mail programs could ignore it and still show the words.

sections.title: Syntax and Line Breaks
sections.content:
Text is in one character set, US-ASCII by default. Every character stands for itself except <, which starts a formatting command. A literal less-than sign is written <<.

A command is a name in angle brackets, at most 60 characters, using only letters, digits and hyphens. A closing form has a slash, as in </bold>, and every opening command must be balanced by one. Commands are case-insensitive, and commands must be properly nested: bold then italic must close italic first.

Line breaks follow special rules. An isolated CRLF becomes a single space, and N consecutive CRLFs become N-1 line breaks. When sending, isolated breaks should be added to keep each line shorter than 80 characters. This lets long paragraphs wrap naturally despite line wrapping by mailers.
sections.plainLanguage: Words in angle brackets are instructions, not text. A single press of Enter is treated as a space, and a blank line means a real new line.

sections.title: The Formatting Commands
sections.content:
Font commands are bold, italic, underline, fixed, fontfamily, color, smaller and bigger. Colors can be named (red, blue, green, yellow, cyan, magenta, black, white) or given as three 4-digit hexadecimal values. Size changes of two points are recommended.

Layout commands are center, flushleft, flushright, flushboth, paraindent and nofill. Each forces a line break before and after. Markup commands are excerpt for quoted text and lang for language tags. The param command carries a parameter for another command and is not shown to the reader. The older Indent and IndentRight commands are deprecated.

Not every implementation will support every command. Missing support should never stop text from being displayed. Unrecognized commands MUST be treated as no-ops, and private extensions may start with X-.
sections.plainLanguage: There is a small menu of tricks: make words bold, slanted, colored, centered or pushed in. If a program does not know a trick, it just skips it.

sections.title: Character Sets and Minimal Support
sections.content:
Any legal MIME charset can be used. Formatting cannot cross MIME body part boundaries, so text needing several different non-ASCII character sets in one paragraph should use a single part with a charset that covers everything, such as UNICODE-1-1-UTF-7. Otherwise a multipart message can hold several text/enriched parts, each starting in the initial state with all commands balanced.

The commands themselves are always the ASCII ones, so before a command the prevailing character set should be switched back into ASCII, and only characters that would be read as < in plain text start commands.

A minimal implementation converts << to <, removes everything from a param command to its closing command, removes all other angle-bracket commands, and applies the CRLF rules outside nofill. A fancier mail program can offer text/enriched inside multipart/alternative next to a richer format.
sections.plainLanguage: Even a very simple reader can just throw away the tags and keep the words, and the message still makes sense.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: The RFC says that security issues are not discussed in this memo, as the mechanism raises no security issues. That is its entire statement on the subject.
sections.plainLanguage: The authors say these simple tags cause no safety worries, and they leave it at that.

data.title: A short text/enriched body
data.code:
Content-type: text/enriched

<bold>Now</bold> is the time for <italic>all</italic>
good men to come to the aid of
their <color><param>red</param>beloved</color> country.
